# Rotational Instabilities and Black Hole Formation in Relativistic Stars

This study examines how rotational instabilities influence the formation of black holes in relativistic stars. Rotation plays a fundamental role in determining the dynamical behavior of collapsing stellar objects, and the manner in which instabilities develop can significantly alter both the pathway and the outcome of gravitational collapse.

In the standard scenario, black hole formation proceeds through an axially symmetric dynamical instability. In this case, the collapse preserves the axial symmetry of the star, leading to the formation of an event horizon at the star's center. This represents the classical picture of how relativistic stars collapse to produce black holes, with matter falling inward symmetrically toward the rotational axis.

Recent research, however, has revealed a more complex set of possibilities. Newly discovered low-$T/|W|$ instabilities—which can develop even when the ratio of rotational kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy is relatively small—can trigger fundamentally different collapse dynamics in differentially rotating stars. Rather than maintaining axial symmetry, these instabilities can cause the star to fragment, resulting in the formation of horizons away from the central axis. This off-center horizon formation departs markedly from the traditional collapse picture and introduces new channels through which black holes may emerge.

This fragmentation process is of particular astrophysical significance, as it may offer an alternative pathway for producing supermassive black holes from supermassive stars. Instead of forming a single central black hole through symmetric collapse, the fragmentation induced by low-$T/|W|$ instabilities could lead to distinct collapse dynamics and multiple sites of horizon formation, thereby reshaping our understanding of how the most massive black holes originate.

This alternative pathway is especially relevant for stars in which angular momentum transport is inefficient. When angular momentum cannot be redistributed effectively throughout the star, differential rotation is maintained, providing the conditions under which low-$T/|W|$ instabilities can develop and drive fragmentation. In such systems, the alternative collapse mechanism becomes a plausible and important route to supermassive black hole formation.

# Rotational Instabilities and Black Hole Formation in Relativistic Stars

## Introduction

The formation of black holes through the gravitational collapse of rotating relativistic stars remains one of the central problems in relativistic astrophysics. Rotation introduces a rich dynamical landscape, since the interplay between gravity, pressure, and centrifugal support can trigger a variety of instabilities that fundamentally alter the collapse process and the properties of the resulting compact object. In this work, we investigate the role of rotational instabilities during black hole formation, focusing on two distinct classes of phenomena: the classical, axially symmetric dynamical instabilities that have long been studied in the context of stellar collapse, and the more recently discovered low-$T/|W|$ instabilities that arise in differentially rotating configurations.

## Two Classes of Rotational Instability

Rotating stars are characterized in part by the ratio of their rotational kinetic energy $T$ to their gravitational binding energy $|W|$. Traditional stability analyses identify a *dynamical bar-mode instability* that sets in when this ratio exceeds a critical threshold of approximately $T/|W| \approx 0.27$. Above this value, the star is unstable to non-axisymmetric ($m=2$) deformations that develop on a dynamical timescale, driving the system toward an elongated, bar-like configuration. This instability is largely independent of the detailed rotation profile and represents the standard channel through which rapidly rotating stars break axial symmetry.

In contrast, the *low-$T/|W|$ instability* operates at values of the energy ratio well below the classical threshold, sometimes as low as $T/|W| \sim 0.01$–$0.1$. This instability is not a global dynamical instability in the traditional sense but is instead associated with the presence of differential rotation and, in particular, with the existence of a corotation point where the pattern speed of an unstable mode matches the local angular velocity of the fluid. Because it depends sensitively on the rotation law, the low-$T/|W|$ instability is especially relevant for stars in which angular momentum is not efficiently redistributed and strong differential rotation can be sustained.

## Numerical Investigation

To explore these instabilities in the strong-field regime, we perform fully general relativistic simulations of collapsing rotating stars, evolving both the spacetime geometry and the relativistic hydrodynamics self-consistently. By systematically varying the initial rotation profile, the degree of differential rotation, and the compactness of the progenitor, we are able to track the growth of non-axisymmetric perturbations, monitor the redistribution of mass and angular momentum, and follow the process of apparent horizon formation.

Our simulations confirm the expected behavior for the standard axisymmetric dynamical instabilities and reproduce the onset of bar-mode deformation in rapidly and near-uniformly rotating models. More importantly, they reveal the qualitatively different outcomes that arise when the low-$T/|W|$ instability is active in strongly differentially rotating stars.

## Fragmentation and Off-Center Horizon Formation

We find that in differentially rotating configurations, the low-$T/|W|$ instability can grow rapidly and drive the star toward *fragmentation*, in which the collapsing matter breaks up into two or more dense clumps rather than collapsing coherently about a single center. As these fragments accrete matter and deepen their gravitational potential wells, apparent horizons can form *off-center*, away from the original rotation axis of the star. This off-center and potentially multiple horizon formation represents a striking departure from the standard picture of monolithic, axially symmetric collapse to a single central black hole.

Such behavior has direct consequences for the dynamics and observational signatures of the collapse, including the emission of gravitational radiation. The non-axisymmetric mass distribution associated with fragmentation and bar-like deformation acts as an efficient source of gravitational waves, offering a potential means of distinguishing these instability channels in future observations.

## Implications for Supermassive Black Hole Formation

Perhaps the most significant implication of these results concerns the origin of supermassive black holes. The existence of billion-solar-mass black holes at high redshift poses a serious challenge to standard formation scenarios, since there is limited cosmic time available to grow such objects from stellar-mass seeds through accretion alone. One attractive alternative is the *direct collapse* of supermassive stars, which could provide massive seed black holes early in cosmic history.

Our findings suggest that the low-$T/|W|$ instability may play an important role in this pathway. In supermassive stars where angular momentum transport is inefficient—so that strong differential rotation can be maintained—the low-$T/|W|$ instability provides a mechanism to break axial symmetry, redistribute angular momentum, and shed centrifugal support. Through fragmentation and off-center horizon formation, this process can circumvent the centrifugal barrier that would otherwise inhibit collapse, thereby offering an alternative route to the rapid production of massive black hole seeds.

## Conclusion

Taken together, our results demonstrate that rotational instabilities—both the classical axisymmetric dynamical instabilities and the low-$T/|W|$ instabilities in differentially rotating stars—can profoundly influence the process of black hole formation in relativistic stars. The capacity of the low-$T/|W|$ instability to induce fragmentation and off-center horizon formation, in particular, opens a promising channel for producing supermassive black holes from supermassive stars with inefficient angular momentum transport. Further exploration of the parameter space, combined with more detailed treatments of the relevant microphysics, will be essential for assessing the importance of these instabilities in realistic astrophysical settings.

# Supermassive Black Holes (SMBHs)

Supermassive black holes, commonly abbreviated as SMBHs, are among the most fascinating and enigmatic objects in the universe. This class of black hole is distinguished by its enormous mass, typically ranging from hundreds of thousands to billions of times the mass of our Sun.

## What Are SMBHs?

SMBHs are believed to reside at the centers of most large galaxies, including our own Milky Way. This central position plays a crucial role in the structure and evolution of the galaxies that host them. The supermassive black hole at the heart of the Milky Way, known as Sagittarius A*, contains roughly four million solar masses concentrated within a region smaller than our solar system.

## Formation and Growth

The origin of SMBHs remains one of the great puzzles in modern astrophysics. This is because their immense size is difficult to explain through conventional stellar collapse alone. Scientists propose several theories, including:

- **Direct collapse** of massive gas clouds in the early universe
- **Runaway mergers** of stars in dense stellar clusters
- **Accretion** of matter over billions of years
- **Mergers** between smaller black holes

## Why SMBHs Matter

This category of cosmic object has profound implications for our understanding of the universe. SMBHs influence galactic dynamics, drive powerful jets of energy, and can outshine entire galaxies when actively feeding, appearing as quasars.

## Observational Breakthroughs

In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope captured the first-ever image of a supermassive black hole in galaxy M87. This landmark achievement provided direct visual evidence supporting Einstein's theory of general relativity and opened a new era in the study of these remarkable objects.

Understanding SMBHs continues to be a priority for astronomers, as these giants hold important clues about the birth and evolution of galaxies throughout cosmic history.

# Abstract

We investigate the development of rotational instabilities in rapidly rotating relativistic stars and their role in triggering gravitational collapse to black holes. Using three-dimensional general relativistic hydrodynamic simulations, we examine the dynamical evolution of differentially rotating neutron star models across a range of rotation rates and compactness parameters. Our study focuses on the dynamical bar-mode instability, which develops when the ratio of rotational kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy, $\beta = T/|W|$, exceeds a critical threshold, as well as the lower-threshold secular and low-$T/|W|$ shear instabilities that may operate in more moderately rotating configurations.

We find that stars exceeding the critical value of $\beta \approx 0.27$ undergo rapid non-axisymmetric deformation, producing a characteristic bar-shaped configuration accompanied by the emission of quasi-periodic gravitational radiation. For sufficiently massive and compact progenitors, angular momentum redistribution and the loss of centrifugal support drive the system toward apparent horizon formation, culminating in black hole formation. We characterize the resulting gravitational waveforms, identifying spectral signatures that could distinguish rotational instabilities from other collapse scenarios in observational data from ground-based interferometric detectors.

Our results demonstrate that the interplay between rotational instabilities and relativistic gravity establishes important constraints on the maximum mass and angular momentum of stable neutron star configurations. These findings have direct implications for the interpretation of gravitational wave signals from proto-neutron stars formed in core-collapse supernovae and from the massive remnants produced in binary neutron star mergers. We discuss the sensitivity of our results to the equation of state and initial rotation profile, and outline directions for incorporating magnetic fields and neutrino transport in future work.

---

This process may result in the formation of apparent horizons at off-center locations, particularly when high-density clumps collapse independently of the bulk stellar material. Such off-center black hole formation has implications for gravitational wave signatures and the subsequent merger dynamics of the resulting compact remnants.

# Abstract

The formation of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in the early universe remains a fundamental challenge in astrophysics, particularly given the discovery of billion-solar-mass quasars at redshifts z > 6. Supermassive stars (SMSs) with masses of 10⁴–10⁶ M☉ represent a promising pathway toward "direct collapse" black hole seeds. We review the dynamical instabilities governing the evolution and collapse of these objects. Rotating SMSs are subject to the general relativistic radial instability, which triggers gravitational collapse once the star contracts below a critical adiabatic index threshold near Γ ≈ 4/3, modified by post-Newtonian corrections and rotational support.

Beyond radial collapse, we examine non-axisymmetric instabilities that can redistribute angular momentum and imprint characteristic signatures on the collapse dynamics. While the classical bar-mode instability requires high ratios of rotational-to-gravitational potential energy (T/|W| ≳ 0.27 for dynamical instability), differentially rotating configurations can develop **low-T/|W| instabilities** at substantially lower rotation rates (T/|W| ~ 0.01–0.1). These shear-driven, corotation-resonance instabilities may generate quasi-periodic gravitational wave emission during collapse, offering potential observational signatures accessible to space-based detectors such as LISA and DECIGO.

We further discuss alternative pathways to SMBH formation, including runaway stellar collisions in dense nuclear clusters, the growth of Population III remnants through super-Eddington accretion, and the role of primordial magnetic fields and metal-free atomic-cooling halos in suppressing fragmentation. We highlight the interplay between thermodynamic structure, rotational profile, and the resulting fate—whether direct collapse to a black hole, thermonuclear explosion, or fragmentation into a stellar system. Understanding these instabilities is essential for predicting seed black hole masses, spins, and their multi-messenger signatures.

# Abstract

We present three-dimensional general relativistic hydrodynamic simulations of differentially rotating stars, investigating the nonlinear dynamics of fragmentation instabilities, black hole horizon formation, and angular momentum redistribution across a range of rotation profiles and compactness parameters. Employing a fully constrained formulation of the Einstein field equations coupled to a high-resolution shock-capturing hydrodynamic scheme, we evolve equilibrium configurations constructed with polytropic and tabulated equations of state, systematically varying the degree of differential rotation parameterized by the ratio of central to equatorial angular velocity. Our models span the dynamically unstable regime characterized by high values of the rotational-to-gravitational potential energy ratio (T/|W| ≳ 0.27), where non-axisymmetric bar-mode and one-armed spiral instabilities develop from seeded perturbations.

We find that sufficiently compact, strongly differentially rotating configurations undergo gravitational fragmentation, producing multiple self-gravitating clumps whose subsequent inspiral and merger constitute a viable channel for high-frequency gravitational wave emission. In a subset of models exceeding the critical compactness threshold, individual fragments accrete sufficient rest mass to trigger local gravitational collapse, with apparent horizon formation identified via a fast flow horizon finder. We characterize the resulting quasi-stationary remnants, including massive tori surrounding nascent black holes, and quantify the fraction of baryonic mass and angular momentum retained in the disk versus that captured by the central compact object.

Angular momentum transport is found to be governed principally by non-axisymmetric gravitational torques during the fragmentation phase, redistributing specific angular momentum outward and driving the inner core toward configurations susceptible to collapse. We extract gravitational waveforms and demonstrate that the spectral signatures of fragmentation and horizon formation are potentially distinguishable by next-generation detectors. These results have direct implications for the collapse of massive stellar cores, hypermassive neutron star remnants from binary mergers, and the formation of black hole–torus systems as central engines for gamma-ray bursts.

---

*Keywords:* numerical relativity, differential rotation, gravitational instabilities, black hole formation, gravitational waves, angular momentum transport
